n0001.title: Analog Cognition and Consciousness
n0001.gist: Brain waves, not just synapses and spikes, provide the flexible analog computation that organizes neurons into unified, conscious cognitive states.
n0001.question: What produces flexible, unified cognition and consciousness? (a wave-based theory)

n0012.title: Abstract
n0012.gist: Cognition and consciousness arise from brain waves that organize spiking neurons into flexible, coordinated patterns through analog computation.
n0012.question: What generates cognition and consciousness — the authors' thesis? (one paragraph)

n0015.title: Introduction
n0015.gist: Flexible top-down control cannot be explained by synaptic change alone, so brain waves likely coordinate huge neuron populations to support cognition.
n0015.question: Why can't synapses alone explain flexible top-down control? (a proposed alternative)

n0016.title: The need for fast coordination
n0016.gist: Cognition requires top-down systems that coordinate hundreds of millions of neurons within fractions of a second to align thought with goals.

n0019.title: Limits of synaptic control
n0019.gist: Explaining flexible control through synaptic change alone would require implausibly precise, rapid knowledge of which synapses to coordinate.

n0021.title: Brain waves as the mechanism
n0021.gist: Brain waves, reflecting coordinated circuit activity, both arise from and shape spiking, offering a more plausible control mechanism than synapses alone.

n0023.title: 20th century neuroscience: The classical model of neural information processing
n0023.gist: The classical connectionist model, where each neuron has one fixed function, cannot explain findings that neurons serve many different roles at once.
n0023.question: Why does the connectionist model fail to explain cortical activity? (counterevidence)
n0023.sourceHeading: 20th century neuroscience: The classical model of neural information processing

n0024.title: The connectionist view
n0024.gist: Classical models describe hierarchical feedforward circuits where each neuron has a single, stable, specialized function that never changes.

n0029.title: Evidence against single-function neurons
n0029.gist: Since any task engages about a third of prefrontal neurons, fixed single-function coding would quickly exhaust the brain's capacity, implying neurons must be multifunctional instead.

n0031.title: Mixed Selectivity: Multifunctional neurons enable flexible cognition
n0031.gist: Many cortical neurons multiplex several kinds of information at once, a property called mixed selectivity that demands a flexible routing mechanism beyond fixed synaptic wiring.
n0031.question: Why does mixed selectivity in neurons demand a new control mechanism? (an illustrated example)
n0031.sourceHeading: Mixed Selectivity: Multifunctional neurons enable flexible cognition

n0032.title: Defining mixed selectivity
n0032.gist: Unlike pure object-coding neurons, many prefrontal neurons respond differently to the same object depending on context, such as its order in a sequence.

n0037.title: Why mixed selectivity matters
n0037.gist: Mixed selectivity neurons expand both computational power and storage capacity, representing a core computational principle rather than a minor add-on.

n0039.title: Cortex as overlapping networks
n0039.gist: Because neurons multiplex information, cortex functions as overlapping, shifting networks rather than a fixed mosaic of specialized circuits.

n0041.title: The routing problem
n0041.gist: Dynamically routing signals through overlapping neural networks is hard to explain by synaptic weight changes alone, suggesting brain oscillations may serve this role.

n0043.title: Oscillations organize neural information
n0043.gist: Brain oscillations actively organize, route, and coordinate neural signals across circuits, making them well suited to implement flexible top-down control.
n0043.question: How do oscillations organize and route neural information? (established computational roles)

n0046.title: Oscillations directly influence spiking via ephaptic coupling
n0046.gist: Oscillating electric fields directly and rapidly shape nearby neurons' spiking through ephaptic coupling, offering speed and reach beyond synaptic signaling.
n0046.question: How do electric fields influence spiking without synapses? (a mechanism and its advantages)
n0046.sourceHeading: Oscillations directly influence spiking via ephaptic coupling

n0047.title: Mechanism of ephaptic coupling
n0047.gist: Oscillating extracellular fields directly nudge nearby neurons' membrane potentials, letting synchronized fields recruit and coordinate spiking without using synapses at all.

n0050.title: Advantages over synaptic signaling
n0050.gist: Electric fields spread farther, act on nearly all local neurons continuously, and propagate almost instantaneously, making them suited for rapid large-scale coordination.

n0052.title: Summary of field advantages
n0052.gist: Oscillatory electric fields can align timing, activate or suppress groups of neurons, and flexibly route information to support adaptive top-down control.

n0054.title: Spatial Computing: A theory of oscillatory control of neural information
n0054.gist: Spatially patterned alpha/beta waves act as inhibitory stencils that gate where gamma-band sensory signals can spike, giving the cortex flexible top-down control.
n0054.question: How do brain waves implement flexible top-down control — the Spatial Computing theory? (a proposed mechanism)
n0054.sourceHeading: Spatial Computing: A theory of oscillatory control of neural information

n0055.title: Gamma versus alpha/beta roles
n0055.gist: Gamma rhythms excite spiking while alpha/beta rhythms suppress it, and this push-pull pattern is conserved across species, layers, and many cortical areas.

n0060.title: The stencil mechanism
n0060.gist: Alpha/beta rhythms act as spatial inhibitory stencils over cortex, suppressing gamma-driven spiking in some locations while leaving others open to express feedforward signals.

n0062.title: Flexible reuse without rewiring
n0062.gist: This stencil scheme lets the same neurons be reused for arbitrary tasks simply by changing the control pattern, without the system tracking specific synapses.

n0064.title: Experimental confirmation
n0064.gist: Recordings in primates confirmed that alpha/beta patterns carry learned contextual information that inversely mirrors sensory spiking and predicts behavioral errors.

n0066.title: Why alpha/beta specifically
n0066.gist: The spatial reach of a wave scales with its frequency, and alpha/beta's intermediate scale of a few millimeters appears best suited for top-down control.

n0068.title: Explaining mixed selectivity with spatial computing
n0068.gist: Spatial Computing explains mixed selectivity as context-dependent gating: a neuron's alpha/beta stencil membership shifts across contexts, changing its apparent selectivity.
n0068.question: How does Spatial Computing explain mixed selectivity? (a mechanistic account)
n0068.sourceHeading: Explaining mixed selectivity with spatial computing

n0069.title: Stencils create context-dependent gating
n0069.gist: Each goal creates a unique alpha/beta stencil, so neurons shared across overlapping stencils change their effective selectivity depending on context, producing mixed selectivity.

n0072.title: No need for specialized neurons
n0072.gist: Mixed selectivity needs no fixed context or object neurons; instead broad synaptic connectivity interacts with wave patterns to determine which subpopulations activate when.

n0074.title: Explaining subspace coding with spatial computing
n0074.gist: Spatial Computing explains why coordinated neural populations occupy low-dimensional activity subspaces, with waves segregating distinct contexts into separate, non-interfering patterns.
n0074.question: How does Spatial Computing explain low-dimensional subspace coding? (a mechanistic account)
n0074.sourceHeading: Explaining subspace coding with spatial computing

n0075.title: Mixed selectivity and subspaces
n0075.gist: Mixed selectivity spreads rich information across coordinated neurons, so population activity occupies a lower-dimensional subspace between fully independent and fully pure coding.

n0080.title: Orthogonal subspaces via stencils
n0080.gist: Alpha/beta control signals segregate spiking into overlapping active subsets with structured correlations, which effectively organizes activity into separate, non-interfering subspaces.

n0082.title: Smooth population trajectories
n0082.gist: Population activity traces smooth paths through its subspace over time, possibly because traveling waves continuously pull spiking along a shared trajectory.

n0084.title: Reconciling noisy neurons and ordered populations
n0084.gist: Brain waves offer a tractable way to reconcile noisy, context-dependent single neurons with the structured, low-dimensional behavior seen at the population level.

n0086.title: Traveling Waves and Representational Change
n0086.gist: Traveling waves sweeping across cortex, especially in the alpha/beta band, may drive transitions between different neural coding states underlying cognition.
n0086.question: How do traveling waves change what information neurons represent? (a proposed mechanism)

n0087.title: Traveling waves across cortex
n0087.gist: Brain waves often sweep across cortex as organized traveling waves spanning many frequencies, implicated in perception, attention, memory, and motor control.

n0090.title: Beta waves and movement
n0090.gist: Beta traveling waves act as a brake during stillness and recede at movement onset, coinciding with times when neural representations form or transform.

n0092.title: Waves as state-change signals
n0092.gist: Alpha/beta traveling waves may transition cortical activity between distinct coding subspaces by moving patterns of inhibition and excitation across cortex.

n0095.title: Predictions and alternative framing
n0095.gist: The traveling-wave account predicts wave timing tracks overall activity dynamics rather than specific content, reframing beta's role as a shifting spatial pattern rather than simple suppression.

n0097.title: Theta waves and large-scale coordination
n0097.gist: Slower theta traveling waves may organize activity at a larger scale, coupling with and dragging faster beta and gamma rhythms to influence memory readout.

n0099.title: Analog Computation with Waves
n0099.gist: Brain waves perform genuine analog computation, combining and interfering like physical waves to generate new neural states efficiently and in parallel.
n0099.question: How do brain waves perform computation, not just organization? (analog computing analogy)

n0100.title: What analog computation is
n0100.gist: Analog computing uses continuous physical quantities like wave amplitude and phase, which add, cancel, or combine naturally to solve problems without digital steps.

n0105.title: Analog Computation with Waves
n0105.gist: Historical analog machines and wave physics show that continuous interactions can solve complex equations, a principle that may extend to electric brain waves.

n0108.title: Efficiency of analog computing
n0108.gist: Analog computation evaluates all variables simultaneously throughout a medium, making it inherently parallel and far more energy-efficient than sequential digital computing.

n0110.title: Cortical waves as computing medium
n0110.gist: Overlapping cortical waves of different frequencies and directions can excite or suppress neuron groups, potentially routing and shaping activity like an analog computer.

n0112.title: Combining multiple contexts
n0112.gist: Multiple control signals could combine as summed wave patterns, producing a unique neural activation pattern for every combination of contexts or variables.

n0115.title: Implications for brain efficiency
n0115.gist: Efficient analog wave computation layered atop synaptic storage may explain how the brain computes so much while using only about 20 watts of power.

n0118.title: Altered Cortical Waves and Unconsciousness
n0118.gist: Diverse anesthetic drugs acting on different molecular targets all converge on the same disrupted, slow wave patterns, linking consciousness to large-scale wave organization rather than specific receptors.
n0118.question: What does anesthesia reveal about the basis of consciousness? (convergent evidence across drugs)

n0119.title: Anesthesia disrupts wave dynamics
n0119.gist: General anesthesia does not merely silence cortex but instead profoundly alters its wave dynamics, supporting a central role for waves in consciousness.

n0122.title: Convergence across different drugs
n0122.gist: Despite acting on different molecular targets, various anesthetics all produce similar slow, desynchronized cortical waves that fragment coordinated communication.

n0124.title: Implication for consciousness
n0124.gist: Since different drugs converge on the same systems-level wave disruption, consciousness may depend more on large-scale wave organization than on specific receptors or cells.

n0126.title: A Hybrid Synapse/Wave Framework for Cognition and Consciousness
n0126.gist: Synapses store long-term knowledge while brain waves dynamically determine which representations are active, together generating coordinated cognition and unified conscious experience.
n0126.question: How do synapses and waves jointly produce cognition and consciousness? (an integrative framework)
n0126.sourceHeading: A Hybrid Synapse/Wave Framework for Cognition and Consciousness

n0127.title: Complementary roles of synapses and waves
n0127.gist: Synapses store long-term information while electric fields from spiking feed back to shape spiking itself, creating a loop where waves provide large-scale top-down control.

n0132.title: Experience shapes wave-driven states
n0132.gist: Stored synaptic knowledge combines with ongoing traveling waves through analog computation to generate new brain states, which can then be written back into synaptic wiring.

n0134.title: Waves, binding, and consciousness
n0134.gist: Brain waves dynamically select which stored representations are active, solving the binding problem by linking distributed activity into one unified conscious experience.

n0136.title: Comparison to other theories of consciousness and executive control
n0136.gist: This wave-based theory shares themes with Global Workspace, Integrated Information, Higher-Order, and executive-control theories, but grounds them specifically in analog wave dynamics rather than broadcasting or spikes alone.
n0136.question: How does this wave theory relate to existing theories of consciousness? (comparison across four theories)
n0136.sourceHeading: Comparison to other theories of consciousness and executive control

n0137.title: Workspace and integration theories
n0137.gist: Unlike Global Workspace and Integrated Information theories, this framework locates distributed integration and self-organization in large-scale wave dynamics rather than broadcasting or a specific hot zone.

n0141.title: Higher-order and predictive theories
n0141.gist: Consciousness is reframed as emerging when oscillatory top-down models impose organized structure on lower-level processing, rather than requiring a separate observer system.

n0143.title: Executive control theories
n0143.gist: Unlike theories emphasizing excitatory gating through winner-take-all dynamics, this framework grounds top-down executive control specifically in wave-based analog computation.

n0145.title: Conclusion
n0145.gist: Brain-wide wave dynamics, rather than discrete neural signaling alone, organize cortical activity into the coordinated, energy-efficient states that produce flexible cognition and consciousness.
n0145.question: What ultimately produces unified cognition and consciousness? (closing synthesis)

n0146.title: Waves as organizing principle
n0146.gist: Unlike accounts centered on discrete neurons or circuits, this framework treats brain-wide wave dynamics as the fundamental organizing principle of cognition and consciousness.

n0149.title: Consciousness as integrated wave state
n0149.gist: Consciousness emerges when wave interactions bind distributed neural populations into a globally integrated state while simultaneously performing flexible computation.

n0151.title: Biological plausibility and efficiency
n0151.gist: This wave-based framework requires no special machinery, since cortex naturally generates oscillations, and it is energetically efficient, consistent with evolutionary pressure to minimize computational cost.
